segs: When you're managing user access across
multiple applications, some on premises,
some in the cloud, you need more than
just authentication.
You need a way to provision and
deprovision users consistently,
securely, and automatically.
This is where skimm system for
cross-domain identity management and
application provisioning and Microsoft
intra ID come into play. You use these
tools to automate identity life cycle
management across your hybrid or SAS
landscape.
If you look at the architecture diagram,
you'll notice that Microsoft Entra ID is
right at the center. To the left you
have cloud HR systems like Workday and
SAP success factors. These systems often
act as your source of truth for user
onboarding.
When someone joins your organization,
the HR system records it first. But how
do you ensure that user accounts are
then created in active directory, entra
ID and all the necessary SAS apps like
Dropbox, Atlassian or Box. That's where
SKIM comes in.
SKIM is a standard protocol that allows
identity providers like Microsoft Entra
ID to talk to applications using a
common schema and restful APIs. As an
administrator or developer, you use skim
to build or enable automatic user
provisioning and deprovisioning
pipelines.
Microsoft intra ID acts as the skim
client and the application acts as the
skim server. So whenever a user is
added, updated or removed an entra ID or
the HR system feeding into it, those
changes can automatically reflect in
downstream apps through skim calls.
On the right side of the diagram, you
see apps like Snowflake, Dropbox, Box,
and Atlassian. These are the kinds of
apps that often support SKIM out of the
box. When you integrate them with enter
ID, you don't just provide
authentication and single sign on. You
also ensure that users are created with
the correct attributes, group
memberships, and roles and are removed
promptly when they leave the company.
That's how you enforce identity hygiene
across your environment.
Below Microsoft Entra ID in the diagram,
you see both active directory and on
premises or web apps. Some of these apps
won't support SKIM directly, but you can
still provision users to them via custom
connectors, APIs, or hybrid identity
solutions. In such cases, you may write
application logic or use PowerShell
scripts to mimic SKIM like provisioning
behavior. From a developer perspective,
you might be building an app that your
company or others will use. To make it
SKIM compatible, you implement endpoints
like SL users slashgroups and SLS
schemas as defined by the SKIM 2.0
specification.
You'll use OOTH 2.0 tokens for secure
communication and handle HTTP verbs like
post, patch, and delete to process
identity changes. Once you register your
skim endpoint with Microsoft Entra ID,
it can automatically synchronize user
objects with your app. By using SKIM and
application programming together, you
transform Microsoft Entra ID from just a
login provider into a complete identity
life cycle engine. This means better
security, faster onboarding and fewer
manual processes. Your HR system remains
the system of record. Entra ID acts as
the orchestrator and skim connected apps
become the synchronized targets. So why
does this matter to you as a security or
identity admin? Because every user you
forget to offboard becomes a risk. Every
manually provisioned account increases
overhead. With skim and entra ID, you're
enforcing zero trust principles. Lease
privilege, automated enforcement, and
constant visibility.
